taskforce2004.title: Final Report on the August 14, 2003 Blackout in the United States and Canada: Causes and Recommendations
taskforce2004.author: U.S.-Canada Power System Outage Task Force
taskforce2004.quote: The outage affected an area with an estimated 50 million people and 61,800 megawatts (MW) of electric load in the states of Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania, New York, Vermont, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Jersey and the Canadian province of Ontario. ... Estimates of total costs in the United States range between $4 billion and $10 billion (U.S. dollars). In Canada, gross domestic product was down 0.7% in August ... Shortly after 14:14 EDT, the alarm and logging system in FE's control room failed and was not restored until after the blackout. ... The EMS in service at FE's Ohio control center is a GE Harris (now GE Network Systems) XA21 system. ... 2A) 14:14 EDT: FE alarm and logging software failed. Neither FE's control room operators nor FE's IT EMS support personnel were aware of the alarm failure. ... the FE control room consoles did not receive any further alarms, nor were there any alarms being printed or posted on the EMS's alarm logging facilities. ... From 15:05:41 EDT to 15:41:35 EDT, three 345-kV lines failed with power flows at or below each transmission line's emergency rating. These line trips were not random. Rather, each was the result of a contact between a line and a tree ... ... 2E) 14:41 EDT: The primary FE control system server hosting the alarm function failed. ... 2F) 14:54 EDT: The FE back-up computer failed and all functions that were running on it stopped. ... In the same way that an alarm system can inform operators about the failure of key grid facilities, it can also be set up to alarm them if the alarm system itself fails to perform properly. FE's EMS did not have such a notification system. ... However, because the alarm application moved intact onto the backup while still stalled and ineffective, the backup server failed 13 minutes later, at 14:54 EDT. ... However, for over an hour no one in FE's control room grasped that their computer systems were not operating properly ... operators' screen refresh rates - the rate at which new information and displays are painted onto the computer screen, normally 1 to 3 seconds - slowed to as long as 59 seconds per screen. ... The chart printers continued to scroll but because the underlying computer system was locked up the chart pens showed only the last valid measurement recorded, without any variation. ... leading to the trip and lock-out of FE's Sammis-Star 345-kV line at 16:05:57 Eastern Daylight Time. This was the event that triggered a cascade of interruptions on the high voltage system, causing electrical fluctuations and facility trips such that within seven minutes the blackout rippled from the Cleveland-Akron area across much of the northeast United States and Canada. By 16:13 EDT, more than 508 generating units at 265 power plants had been lost ... 1. Make reliability standards mandatory and enforceable, with penalties for noncompliance.

poulsen2004.title: Tracking the Blackout bug
poulsen2004.author: Kevin Poulsen
poulsen2004.quote: Sometimes working late into the night and the early hours of the morning, the team pored over the approximately one-million lines of code that comprise the XA/21's Alarm and Event Processing Routine, written in the C and C++ programming languages. Eventually they were able to reproduce the Ohio alarm crash in GE Energy's Florida laboratory, says Unum. ... In the end, they had to slow down the system, injecting deliberate delays in the code while feeding alarm inputs to the program. About eight weeks after the blackout, the bug was unmasked as a particularly subtle incarnation of a common programming error called a "race condition," triggered on August 14th by a perfect storm of events and alarm conditions on the equipment being monitoring. The bug had a window of opportunity measured in milliseconds. "There was a couple of processes that were in contention for a common data structure, and through a software coding error in one of the application processes, they were both able to get write access to a data structure at the same time," says Unum. "And that corruption lead to the alarm event application getting into an infinite loop and spinning." ... last fall the company gave its customers a patch against the bug, along with installation instructions and a utility to repair any alarm log data corrupted by the glitch. According to Unum, the company sent the package to every XA/21 customer - more than 100 utilities around the world ... "we had in excess of three million online operational hours in which nothing had ever exercised that bug," says Unum.
supports: Mike Unum, manager of commercial solutions at GE Energy
race condition: two processes with simultaneous write access to one data structure
corruption sent the alarm event application into an infinite loop and spinning
approximately one-million lines of C and C++ in the Alarm and Event Processing Routine
reproduced in GE Energy's Florida laboratory about eight weeks after the blackout, by injecting deliberate delays
patch shipped in autumn 2003 to more than 100 XA/21 utilities
GE Energy made the XA/21 EMS in use at FirstEnergy's control center
scope note: the 'four million lines of C' in the article subhead is the whole EMS; the Alarm and Event Processing Routine is approximately one-million lines. The chapter uses the one-million figure.

epact2005.title: Energy Policy Act of 2005, Public Law 109-58, Sec. 1211 (Electric Reliability Standards)
epact2005.author: 109th United States Congress
epact2005.quote: SEC. 1211. ELECTRIC RELIABILITY STANDARDS. (a) IN GENERAL.-Part II of the Federal Power Act (16 U.S.C. 824 et seq.) is amended by adding at the end the following: "SEC. 215. "(e) ENFORCEMENT.-(1) The ERO may impose, subject to paragraph (2), a penalty on a user or owner or operator of the bulk-power system for a violation of a reliability standard approved by the Commission under subsection (d) if the ERO, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing-

unverified: That FirstEnergy's control room was in Akron, Ohio: neither opened source says so. The Task Force report calls it 'FE's Ohio control center' and its only two uses of 'Akron, Ohio' are ECAR's headquarters and the already-blacked-out area; Poulsen never writes Akron. Cut from the origin box-tag and from card p3c18-c2, which now say Ohio.
The commonly repeated figure of 11 deaths attributed to the blackout: the Task Force Final Report contains no death toll, so the number is not used in the prose.
That Michehl Gent, NERC's president at the time, said anything specific about the alarm failure - no primary transcript was opened, so he is not named.
The exact calendar date on which GE Energy shipped the XA/21 patch: Poulsen reports only 'last fall' relative to April 2004, i.e. autumn 2003.
Whether FirstEnergy's operators would have acted differently with working alarms - the Task Force describes lost situational awareness but does not assert a counterfactual outcome.
